# English for Journalists

### *International Edition*

Student's Book
*A free press, in plain English.*
CEFR A2 → lower B1   ·   10 units   ·   the Atlas Wire world desk

> **A note on real and invented content.** The facts about journalism around the world — the press-freedom indexes, the safety figures, the international days, the codes of ethics, the way accreditation and embargoes work — are true, dated and attributed on the page. Atlas Wire, its staff, the town of Kalina, the river Vara, the crossing and the people in the stories are invented, for practice. Real people and real organisations appear only in true, sourced facts — never in an invented quote.


---


### WELCOME · About this course

English for Journalists · International Edition is a ten-unit English course for journalists who work across borders. You learn English through the work of Atlas Wire, an invented independent news agency with a world desk in Geneva and correspondents in many countries, and through one continuous story: the reopening of the Kalina crossing — from the morning the barrier went up to the front page that told the year.
The course climbs from CEFR A2 to lower B1. Each unit teaches one new piece of grammar and one part of an international journalist's work — from the words of the world desk, to interviews through an interpreter, to attribution, to a full front page.

**How to use this book**

1. Each unit has a Warm-Up and eleven parts: Words, Grammar, a Skill, Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking, Ethics, Digital, Review, and an Assignment.
2. Every part builds up step by step: you see a model, notice how it works, practise it, and then produce your own.
3. Grammar is taught half as controlled practice and half in your own words. Every part mixes exercises you can check with open tasks to discuss and create.
4. The Ethics part in every unit builds the Code: be accurate, be honest, be fair, be independent, and be kind.
5. The Answer Key at the end of each unit gives the answers to the closed exercises. Open tasks (discussion, role-play, and your own writing) are marked.

**The Atlas Wire world desk**

### PART 1 · Newsroom words

*The people, places, and things of an international newsroom. Learn these words first.*

**MODEL** — The words

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| journalist | a person who finds and reports the news |
| correspondent | a journalist who reports from another country |
| stringer | a journalist who sends stories to an outlet, but is not staff |
| editor | a person who checks and prepares stories |
| editor-in-chief | the top editor; the head of the newsroom |
| news agency | a company that sends news to many outlets |
| wire | the stream of stories an agency sends out |
| desk | the team that covers one subject (the world desk) |
| bureau | an agency office in another city or country |
| dateline | the place and date at the top of a report |
| beat | the subject a journalist covers |
| deadline | the time a story must be ready |
| press card | a card that shows you are a journalist |
| fixer | a local journalist who helps a visiting team |

### PART 2 · Grammar in the newsroom

*The present. Half the practice is controlled; half is your own words.*

**MODEL** — The four structures

> **1 · the verb be — am / is / are**
>
> {{I am}} a correspondent.     {{We are}} journalists.
> {{She is}} the world editor.     {{They are}} at the desk.
> Negative: She [[isn't]] a photographer.     Question: [[Are]] you a correspondent?

> **2 · present simple — daily work and facts**
>
> {{I work}} for Atlas Wire.     {{He files}} at six. (he/she/it + -s)
> Correspondents {{report}} from many countries.     She {{writes}} the news.
> Negative: I [[don't]] work Sundays.     Question: [[Do]] you work here?

> **3 · have got — for things you have**
>
> {{I have got}} a notebook.     {{She has got}} a press card.
> Question: [[Have]] you got a visa?

> **4 · there is / there are**
>
> {{There is}} a bureau in Nairobi. (one)     {{There are}} three correspondents. (more than one)
> Negative: There [[isn't]] a photographer today.     Question: [[Is there]] a deadline?

> **Watch out!**  With he / she / it, add -s: *she files* (not *she file*). Use *have got / has got* (not *haves*). Use *there is* for one, *there are* for more than one.

**Structured practice** — half of this part.

### PART 3 · Skill focus: who's who, and the front page

*Different jobs, different beats, and one shared front page.*

**MODEL** — Who does what

> **[FIGURE: `u1-skill`]** — *Figure 1.3 · The editor-in-chief leads. The world editor runs the desk. The team reports, checks, and files.*

> The **editor-in-chief** leads the agency and makes the big decisions.
> The **world editor** chooses the stories and runs the desk.
> A **correspondent** reports from another country, talks to sources, and writes.
> A **field reporter** goes to the place and reports from there, with video.
> A **verification journalist** checks that every fact and every picture is true.
> A **photojournalist** takes the photographs.
> A **digital editor** puts the news online and on social media.

### PART 5 · Read the story

*Two readings. Reading A is a true report about the world's press. Reading B is a staff profile.*

**Reading A** · factual · current

**NOTICE** — Before you read

**5A**  Talk with a partner.

1. How do you get news from other countries: TV, radio, or online?
2. Do you know any international news agencies?
3. What makes a good correspondent? Say one thing.

> **A free press, around the world**
>
> Journalism crosses borders. A story that starts in one country is read in fifty. This is big news for journalists, and for everyone.
> Every year, Reporters Without Borders publishes the World Press Freedom Index. It ranks 180 countries and territories. Some countries rise; some countries fall. The Index does not say that one country is good and another is bad. It asks a simpler question: can a journalist do the work, and is the journalist safe?
> In many places, the answer is still no. Every year on 1 December, the Committee to Protect Journalists counts the journalists who are in prison for their work. In recent years, that number has been more than three hundred. UNESCO reports that when a journalist is killed, nobody is punished in about nine of every ten cases.
> There is also good news. In 1991, journalists met in Windhoek and wrote a declaration for a free press. In 1993, the United Nations named 3 May World Press Freedom Day. In 2012, the United Nations agreed a Plan of Action on the Safety of Journalists. And 2 November is now the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists.
> Journalists also work together. Reporters in many countries share documents and check each other's facts. One story, forty newsrooms, one deadline: this is normal now.
> The work is the same in every language. Find the story. Check the facts. Name the source. Be fair, and be kind. A free press is not a building. It is a habit — and journalists keep it, together.

> **[FIGURE: `u1-read`]** — *Figure 1.7 · Journalists in prison for their work, counted every 1 December. Source: Committee to Protect Journalists.*

### PART 8 · Ethics & the Code

*Good English is not enough. A good journalist follows the rules of the job.*

**MODEL** — A case, and the Code

> **A case.** Mira is at the crossing at Kalina. She writes a good story about the market on the bridge. An official is very happy with the story. "Your story is beautiful," he says. "Please write only good things about the crossing. Here — we will pay for your flight and your hotel next time." He puts an envelope in her hand. Mira likes the official, and the agency has little money. But she is a journalist. She knows the Code: a journalist is independent, and does not take money to change a story. What does Mira do? What does she say to the official?

|   |   |
|---|---|
| **Accuracy** — The facts are correct. | **Fairness** — You give more than one side. |
| **Honesty** — You tell the truth. | **Respect** — You treat people well. |

*A fifth idea — independence — means no one controls your news. These ideas appear in codes of ethics all over the world, among them the IFJ Global Charter of Ethics for Journalists (2019).*

**PRACTISE** — Understand the values

> **[FIGURE: `u1-ethA`]** — *A case — an official offers a paid trip; a journalist stays independent.*

Atlas Wire, its staff, Kalina, the crossing, the Meridian Post and Omar are invented, for practice. In this course, real people are only ever in true, sourced facts — never in an invented quote.

## UNIT 2 · What Is News? The Five Ws

*ENGLISH FOR JOURNALISTS · INTERNATIONAL EDITION · STUDENT'S BOOK*

**Beat · Report & newswriting        CEFR A2**

**In this unit you learn to…**

- ask the five Ws — and How — about a story
- tell hard news from soft news
- describe a story with the right adjectives
- use wh- questions and the present simple for facts
- write 5-W notes and pitch a story idea

### PART 1 · Newsroom words

*The words you need to talk about news and stories. Learn these first.*

**MODEL** — The words

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| news | information about new events |
| story | a report about one event or subject |
| event | a thing that happens |
| angle | the main idea of a story; what is new |
| fact | a thing that is true |
| detail | a small piece of information |
| report | a written or spoken news story |
| source | a person or place that gives information |
| hard news | important news, now (politics, prices, safety) |
| soft news | interesting but not urgent news (culture, sport) |
| important | that matters a lot |
| local | in your city or area |
| international | in more than one country |
| main | the biggest or most important |

### PART 2 · Grammar: questions & describing

*Ask about a story, and describe it. Half the practice is controlled; half is your own words.*

**MODEL** — The grammar

> **1 · wh- question words — the five Ws + How**
>
> {{Who}} = people     {{What}} = the thing / event
> {{When}} = the time     {{Where}} = the place
> {{Why}} = the reason     {{How}} = the way

> **2 · asking a question**
>
> With *be*:  [[Wh + is/are + …?]]   What is the news?   Where is the crossing?
> With other verbs:  [[Wh + do/does + subject + verb?]]   When does the crossing open?   Why do families come back?

> **3 · adjectives — describing a story**
>
> Before the noun:  a {{big}} story · an {{important}} event · {{international}} news
> After *be*:  The story is {{important}}. The bridge is {{busy}}.

> **Watch out!**  In a question, the wh- word comes first: *What is the news?* (not *The news is what?*). The adjective does not change: two big *storys* → two big *stories*, but *big* stays *big*.

**Structured practice** — half of this part.

**NOTICE** — Which question word?

> **[FIGURE: `u2-gA`]** — *The question words — who, what, when, where, why, how.*

**5A**  What kinds of stories are in the news in your country? Name two.

> **What is news around the world today?**
>
> Open any international news website, and the stories are not all the same size. Some news is about big change. People move. Borders open and close. Governments meet, and agree, or do not agree. This is important news for many people, in many countries at once.
> Other news is about daily life. Prices go up and down. A new clinic opens. A school starts again. A bridge reopens, and a market comes back with it. People want this news, too — and often they want it more.
> There is also soft news — sport, music, and culture. A football match, a new song, a festival: these are stories too, and they cross borders easily.
> For a journalist, the job is the same in every country. Find the story. Ask the five Ws. Check the facts. Name the source. The subject changes; the work does not.

### PART 8 · Ethics & the Code: get the facts right

*A story must be true. Check every fact before you report it.*

**MODEL** — A case

> **A case.** A post online says "a thousand people crossed today" at Kalina. But Mira is on the bridge, and she counts about three hundred. Which number does she report?

> The Code says: **be accurate**. A **fact** is true. A **rumour** is a story with no proof. An **opinion** is what someone thinks. Report facts. Check them with a source.

**PRACTISE** — Fact or opinion?

> **[FIGURE: `u2-ethA`]** — *Fact or opinion? A fact is true; an opinion is what someone thinks.*

6. This is the most important news of the year. ___________

2. "Maybe a thousand crossed." (no proof) ___________

4. "The market opens at six o'clock." ___________

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8C**  Choose (a) or (b).

2. A person gives you a fact. (a) use it now (b) ask "How do you know?" ______
3. You have one source. (a) file the story (b) find a second source. ______

**PRACTISE** — Complete the rule

**8D**  Complete with: fact · know · source · rumour.

She did not see five hundred stalls. Maybe it is true, but maybe it is only a rumour. The deadline is soon, and a big number is good news. But Mira is a journalist. ### PART 11 · Assignment: find a story

#### Find a story and take its 5-W notes

Choose a real story from another country (or invent one). Do these three things:

1. write **5-W notes** (Who, What, When, Where, Why, How);
2. say if it is **hard or soft** news;
3. write a **one-line pitch** with the angle.

> Plan: ask the six questions first; check your facts with a source.

## UNIT 3 · Live from the Scene: Reporting Now

**Beat · Report & live**  ·  CEFR A2 → lower B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. describe what is happening now (present continuous)
2. talk about plans with going to
3. say where people and things are (prepositions of place)
4. report a short live update from a scene

> **[FIGURE: `g-team`]** — *The Atlas Wire team — Mira reports live in this unit.*

**The story so far.** The crossing at Kalina is open again. Today Mira is at the bridge, reporting live for the wire and for radio. She tells us what is happening now, and what is going to happen next.

### PART 1 · Live: the words of the scene

*The words a reporter needs at the scene. Learn these first.*

> **[FIGURE: `u3-words`]** — *Four key words — live, scene, crowd, update.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| live | news as it happens, now |
| scene | the place a story happens |
| report | a story; to tell the news |
| microphone | a reporter speaks into it |
| crowd | many people together |
| happening | going on now |
| plan | what you are going to do |
| cover | to report a story |
| on air | being shown or heard now |
| update | new information |
| breaking | very new and important |
| event | a thing that happens |
| moment | a very short time |
| broadcast | to send news on TV or radio |

### PART 2 · Grammar: now and next

*Present continuous for now, going to for plans, and prepositions for place.*

> **[FIGURE: `u3-gA`]** — *Present continuous — am / is / are + verb-ing = happening now.*

> **1 · Present continuous — happening now**
>
> Form: {{am / is / are}} + verb{{-ing}}.
> Mira {{is reporting}}.   People {{are crossing}}.   The stalls {{are opening}}.
> We use it for things that are happening now, at this moment.

> **2 · going to — plans and the future**
>
> Form: {{am / is / are}} + {{going to}} + verb.
> She {{is going to}} interview a stall-holder.   We {{are going to}} cover the story.
> We use it for plans and what we think will happen next.

> **[FIGURE: `u3-gB`]** — *Prepositions of place — in, at, next to, in front of.*

> **3 · Prepositions of place**
>
> {{in}} a place: The town is {{in}} the valley.
> {{at}} a point: Mira is {{at}} the crossing.
> {{next to}} / {{in front of}} / {{behind}}: The café is {{next to}} the bridge.

### PART 5 · Reading: from the field

*Two readings. Read for what is happening, and for the plan.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-notes`]** — *Live updates in brief — short items from the field.*

**Reading A** · a live report, written down

> **A busy morning at the Kalina crossing**
>
> It is nine o'clock, and the crossing at Kalina is waking up. The barrier is up, the stalls are open, and a big crowd is here. Correspondent Mira Sandoval is standing at the old gate with a microphone.
> "This is a very busy morning," Mira says. "People are carrying bags and boxes across the bridge. Families are coming from both sides of the river, and children are running ahead of them. Next to the gate, a young family is opening a small café. This is their first day."
> Behind Mira, a stall-holder is putting fruit on his table. He is smiling. "The people are coming back," he says. "Every morning, more families cross. It is good for business, and it is good for the valley."
> At the end of the bridge, a group of workers is painting the rail. "We are getting the crossing ready," one worker says. "Next week, there is going to be a small festival here, on both sides."
> A little further on, two teachers are standing in front of the new school bus. They are waiting for the children. "We are starting again today," one teacher says. "Forty children are coming this morning, and more are coming next week. It is a very happy day for us."
> Near the barrier, an old man is watching the crowd. He is not shopping; he is just looking. "For seven years, this bridge was closed and quiet," he says slowly. "Now it is full of people again. I am very happy. I am coming here every morning now, just to see the families."
> Mira looks at the camera. "So the news this morning is simple and happy: Kalina is open. In a moment, I am going to talk to the family at the new café. This is Mira Sandoval, live from the crossing. Back to you in the studio."

> **[FIGURE: `u3-read`]** — *Say where you are, say what is happening, say what is next — then stop.*

**Reading B** · reporting from the field — three tips

> **Three tips for a live report**
>
> **1. Say where you are.** Start with the place: 'This is Mira Sandoval, live from the crossing at Kalina.' The listener is far away and needs to see the scene.
> **2. Say what is happening now.** Use the present continuous: 'The stalls are opening. A crowd is crossing.' Talk about this moment, not last week.
> **3. Say what is next.** Use *going to* for the plan: 'In a moment, I am going to talk to a stall-holder.' This keeps the listener with you.
> And always: stay calm, speak clearly, and only say what you can see. Do not guess.

### PART 8 · Ethics: live and fair

*Live news is fast. A journalist is still accurate and kind.*

> **[FIGURE: `u3-ethA`]** — *On air, still say only what you can see — a fact, not a guess.*

**A first case** · a number you cannot see

> **A case.** Mira is live at the crossing. The studio asks her: "How many people are there?" Mira can see a big crowd, but she did not count them. A voice in her ear says, "Just say ten thousand — it sounds good." The report is live, and listeners in many countries are hearing it now. But Mira did not count ten thousand people. She is a journalist, and she knows the Code: report only what you can see, and do not guess a number as a fact. What does Mira say on air?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8A**  Choose (a) or (b), and write one reason.

4. "Everyone in the valley is here." ______

**PRACTISE** — Apply the Code

**A second case** · filming an upset person

> **[FIGURE: `u3-ethB`]** — *Respect people — ask before you film, even on a busy day.*

> **A case.** Tomas is filming the crowd for the live report. He sees a woman at the barrier who is crying. It is a strong picture, and the deadline is now. But the woman does not want to be on camera. She turns away and puts up her hand. Tomas needs pictures for the report, and the pictures will go out in many countries. But the woman said no. The Code says: respect people, and ask before you film. What does Tomas do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**PRODUCE** — Discuss

|---|---|

| polite | kind and respectful |

### PART 2 · Grammar: asking politely

*Can and could for requests, would for offers, and the order of a question.*

> **[FIGURE: `u4-gA`]** — *Can, could and would make a question polite.*

> **1 · can / could — requests**
>
> {{can}}: {{Can I}} ask you a question?   {{Can you}} say that again?
> {{could}} is more polite: {{Could you}} tell me your name, please?
> Use them to ask for permission and to make a request.

> **2 · would — offers and polite requests**
>
> {{Would you like}} to talk to me?   (an offer / a soft request)
> {{Would you}} say a little more, please?
> *would* is gentle and very polite.

> **[FIGURE: `u4-gB`]** — *A question: (wh-) + do / can / is + subject + verb + ?*

> **3 · Question forms**
>
> Yes / no: [[Do]] you live here?   [[Is]] the crossing open?   [[Can]] I record this?
> Wh-: [[What do]] you do?   [[Where do]] you live?   [[Why did]] you come back?
> Order: (wh-) + do / does / can / is + subject + verb + ?

### PART 5 · Reading: the interview

*Two readings. Read for the questions and the quotes.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *A short interview, written up for the wire.*

**Reading A** · an interview, written up

> **'My mother is on the other side': a family comes back to Kalina**
>
> This week, correspondent Mira Sandoval sat down with Elena Marku and her family at their new café, at the end of the bridge at Kalina. The family came back to the town last month, and they are already part of the street.
> "Could you tell me why you came back?" Mira asked. Elena smiled. "It is our home," she said. "We were away for seven years, but we always wanted to come back. When we heard that the crossing was open again, we knew it was time. My mother is on the other side of the river. Now I can see her every day."
> Mira asked what they were going to do. "We are going to run this little café," Elena said. "My husband makes the coffee, and I make the bread. Our children help after school. Every day, more neighbours come and sit with us."
> The café is small — only six tables — but it is always full. "People do not only come for coffee," Elena said. "They come to talk, and to see old friends. The valley is waking up, and we are happy to be a part of it."
> Dren, a journalist from the town, sat with them and helped when the English was difficult. "People here want to tell their own story," he said afterwards. "They only need somebody to ask properly."
> Before she left, Mira asked one more question. "Would you like to say anything to your neighbours?" Elena laughed. "Yes," she said. "Please come and visit us. The door is always open, and the coffee is always hot."

> **[FIGURE: `u4-read`]** — *Prepare, be polite, listen, and get the quote exactly right.*

**Reading B** · preparing for an interview — four tips

> **Four tips for a good interview**
>
> **1. Prepare your questions.** Write three or four questions before you go. Mix wh- questions and yes/no questions.
> **2. Be polite.** Start with a request: 'Can I ask you a question?' Use *could* and *would*. Say please and thank you.
> **3. Listen well.** Do not only read your questions. Listen to the answer, and ask a follow-up: 'Could you say more about that?'
> **4. Get the quote right.** Write the person's exact words. If you work with an interpreter, ask them to translate word for word, and check anything you are not sure of. Do not change what the guest said.

### PART 8 · Ethics: a fair interview

*An interview is a promise: report what the guest really said.*

> **[FIGURE: `u4-ethA`]** — *Report the guest's exact words — do not change them to sound better.*

**A first case** · changing the quote

> **A case.** After the interview, Elena calls Mira. "I have thought about it," she says. "Can you make my answer sound better? Please write that my café is the best in the region, and that hundreds of people come every day." But Elena did not say that in the interview, and it is not true. Mira wrote down Elena's real words: 'It is our home, and the coffee is always hot.' Mira likes Elena and wants to help. But she is a journalist, and she knows the Code: report what the guest really said, and do not print things that are not true. What does Mira do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

> **A case.** During the interview, a guest tells Mira something sad about the seven years when the crossing was closed. Then he says, "Please do not put that in the story. I only wanted you to understand. It is private." It is a strong story, and it would travel far on the wire. But the guest asked Mira not to use it. The Code says: respect people, and keep your promise. What does Mira do?

### PART 1 · The words of the quote

*The words a reporter needs to report what people said. Learn these first.*

> **[FIGURE: `u5-words`]** — *Four key words — attribution, statement, confirm, spokesperson.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| quote | a person's exact words |
| source | a person who gives information |
| attribution | saying who said it |
| statement | an official thing someone says |
| claim | to say something is true (maybe not sure) |
| confirm | to say yes, it is true |
| deny | to say no, it is not true |
| add | to say one more thing |
| explain | to make something clear |
| mention | to say something quickly |
| spokesperson | a person who speaks for a group |
| agency | an organisation that does official work |
| accurate | correct, with no mistakes |
| exact | just right; the same words |

### PART 2 · Grammar: reporting what people said

*say and tell, reported speech, and attribution.*

> **[FIGURE: `u5-gA`]** — *say (that)… / tell + a person + (that)…*

> **1 · say and tell**
>
> {{say}} (that)… — no person: She {{said}} (that) the crossing {{was}} open.
> {{tell}} + a person + (that)…: She {{told me}} (that) it {{was}} open.
> Remember: we **tell somebody**, but we **say something**.

> **[FIGURE: `u5-gB`]** — *Direct words become reported speech — the tense moves back.*

> **2 · Reported speech**
>
> Direct: "The crossing {{is}} open."  →  Reported: He said the crossing {{was}} open.
> Direct: "We {{are}} happy."  →  She said they {{were}} happy.
> The tense moves back: [[is → was]], [[are → were]], [[am → was]].

> **3 · Attribution**
>
> Always say who a fact comes from.
> {{According to}} the Crossing Office, a hundred families have crossed back.
> The spokesperson {{said}} that the bridge {{was}} open.  A stall-holder {{told}} Mira it {{was}} busy.

### PART 5 · Reading: what people said

*Two readings. Read for the quotes and the sources.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *A report is built from what people said — with their names.*

**Reading A** · a report with quotes

> **Voices from the Kalina crossing**
>
> This week, correspondent Mira Sandoval spoke to many people at the crossing at Kalina. They all had something to say about the bridge that is open again.
> Elena Marku, who owns the new café at the end of the bridge, told Mira that business was good. "The café is always full," she said. "People do not only come for coffee. They come to talk, and to see old friends."
> A stall-holder on the bridge said that families crossed every morning. According to him, the market was busy from early until late. "Every day, I see new faces," he added.
> The Crossing Office made a short statement. According to the office, a hundred families have now returned to the valley, and the school will open next week. The office also said that a small festival is planned for Friday.
> Not everyone agreed on the numbers. One worker told Mira that he thought there were more than a hundred families. Another said there were fewer. Mira wrote down both, and she used the office's figure, with attribution, for the story.
> Priya Nair, the verification journalist at Atlas Wire, said that this was the right thing to do. "We report what people say," she explained, "but we always name the source. If two people say different things, we say so. We do not choose one and hide the other. On an international story that goes out in six languages, that matters even more: a number with no name behind it travels a very long way."

> **[FIGURE: `u5-read`]** — *Name the source, use say and tell correctly, move the tense back, keep it exact.*

**Reading B** · say it right — four rules for quotes

> **Four rules for quotes**
>
> **1. Name your source.** For every fact and every number, say who said it: 'according to…' or '… said'.
> **2. Use say and tell correctly.** You *say* something; you *tell* somebody. 'She said that…' or 'She told me that…'.
> **3. Change the tense.** In reported speech, the tense moves back: 'is' becomes 'was', 'are' becomes 'were'.
> **4. Keep it accurate.** Use the person's exact words in a quote. Do not change what they said. If the interview was in another language, keep the translation close and say that it is a translation. If two sources disagree, report both.

### PART 8 · Ethics: fair and sourced

*Report what people said — all of it, and always with a source.*

> **[FIGURE: `u5-ethA`]** — *When two sources disagree, report both — do not choose one and hide the other.*

**A first case** · two sources disagree

> **A case.** Mira asks about the number of families. A stall-holder tells her that a hundred families have come back. But a worker says there are only fifty. The two sources do not agree. The story is due soon, and a bigger number sounds better on an international wire. Mira could just write 'a hundred families' and leave out the worker. But two people said different things. The Code says: be accurate and fair — report what each source said, and name them. What does Mira do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8A**  Choose (a) or (b), and write one reason.

1. (a) write only the bigger number  (b) report both, with the office's figure and attribution.   Choice: ______  Because ________________________
2. When two sources disagree, a reporter should (a) hide one  (b) report both.   Choice: ______

**8B**  Fair or not fair? Write F (fair) or U (unfair).

1. Report both numbers, and name the sources. ______
2. Print only the number you like. ______
3. Use the official figure, with attribution. ______
4. Hide the source that disagrees. ______

**PRACTISE** — Apply the Code

**PRODUCE** — Discuss

**8D**  Discuss. Why is it unfair to report only one side? Who does it hurt?

**A second case** · 'do not use my name'

> **[FIGURE: `u5-ethB`]** — *A claim with no name needs a second source before you report it.*

> **A case.** A person tells Mira something important about the crossing, but says, "Do not use my name." It is a big claim, and it could be a strong story on the wire. But Mira has only one source, and that source will not be named. She cannot write 'according to…' because she cannot say who. The Code says: check a claim with a second source before you report it, and be careful with information you cannot attribute. What does Mira do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

## UNIT 6 · Telling the Story: What Happened

**Beat · Report & feature**  ·  CEFR A2 → lower B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. tell what happened (past simple)
2. describe what was happening (past continuous)
3. use time words (ago, last, when, while)
4. write a short news story about a past event

### PART 2 · Grammar: the past

*Past simple for the events, past continuous for the background.*

> **[FIGURE: `u6-gA`]** — *Past simple — the events, one after another.*

> **1 · Past simple — what happened**
>
> Regular: add {{-ed}}: open → {{opened}}, return → {{returned}}, start → {{started}}.
> Irregular: come → {{came}}, go → {{went}}, be → {{was / were}}, say → {{said}}, build → {{built}}.
> The crossing {{opened}} last spring.  Families {{came}} back.  It {{was}} a happy day.

> **[FIGURE: `u6-gB`]** — *Past continuous — what was happening in the background.*

> **2 · Past continuous — what was happening**
>
> Form: {{was / were}} + verb{{-ing}}.
> When Mira arrived, people {{were crossing}} and children {{were running}}.
> Use it for the background — a longer action that was going on.

> **3 · Time words**
>
> {{ago}}: seven years {{ago}}.   {{last}}: {{last}} week / {{last}} spring.   {{yesterday}}.
> {{when}} + past simple: {{When}} the barrier went up, people were waiting.
> {{while}} = at the same time: {{While}} the workers repaired the road, families returned.

### PART 5 · Reading: the feature

*Two readings. Read for the events and the order.*

> **[FIGURE: `u6-read`]** — *A feature tells the whole story — from how it was, to how it is.*

**Reading A** · a feature about the seven years

> **The year the crossing came back**
>
> Seven years ago, the bridge at Kalina closed. The barrier came down one evening, and it stayed down. The road was empty. The stalls disappeared. The old gate at the end of the bridge rusted in the rain, and for a long time the only sound on the river was the water.
> Then, last spring, things began to change. First, a small team of workers arrived and looked at the bridge. While they were measuring the rail, people on both sides watched them from their windows. Nobody said very much, but everybody understood.
> The repairs took four months. Workers rebuilt the road surface and painted the rail. In April, the barrier went up. "I opened my stall for the first time in seven years," one stall-holder remembered. "While I was setting up, families started to arrive. Everyone was smiling."
> When the school bus crossed the bridge in the autumn, forty children returned to class on the other side. Their teacher said that it was the happiest day of the year. After that, more stalls opened, and a young family started a small café at the end of the bridge.
> Today, the crossing is busy again. According to the Crossing Office, a hundred families have now returned to the valley. "For seven years, we were waiting," Elena Marku, the café owner, said. "Now the door is open, and the coffee is hot. The valley came back."

**Reading B** · writing a story about the past — four tips

> **Four tips for a past story**
>
> **1. Use the past simple for the events.** What happened, one thing after another: 'The crossing opened. Families came back.'
> **2. Use the past continuous for the background.** What was going on at the time: 'While the workers were painting, families were arriving.'
> **3. Use time words to show the order.** 'Seven years ago… Then… When… After that…' The reader follows the story.
> **4. Keep it accurate.** Check the dates and the numbers. Name a source. Use the eyewitness's exact words in a quote.

### PART 8 · Ethics: a true story

*A story about the past must still be accurate and kind.*

> **[FIGURE: `u6-ethA`]** — *Report what you can confirm — not what sounds bigger.*

**A first case** · the number grows

> **A case.** Mira is writing the story of the day the crossing reopened. One stall-holder tells her, "I think ten thousand people crossed that day — maybe more!" It makes a great line, and the story is due soon. But nobody counted, and the Crossing Office says the real number was much smaller. Mira cannot confirm ten thousand. She is a journalist, and she knows the Code: report what you can confirm, and do not make a past event bigger than it was. What does Mira write?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8A**  Choose (a) or (b), and write one reason.

1. (a) write 'ten thousand people crossed'  (b) write 'many people crossed' (what she can confirm).   Choice: ______  Because ________________________
2. A number nobody counted is (a) a fact  (b) not confirmed.   Choice: ______

**8B**  Can you confirm it? Write Y (yes) or N (no).

1. The crossing reopened last spring (the office confirms it). ______
2. Exactly ten thousand people crossed (nobody counted). ______
3. Families were arriving all morning (many saw it). ______
4. It was the biggest day in the valley's history. ______

**PRACTISE** — Apply the Code

**8C**  Complete the rule. Use: confirm · bigger · true · check.

> Tell a ______ story. Only write what you can ______ . ______ the dates and numbers, and do not make a past event ______ than it was.

**PRODUCE** — Discuss

**8D**  Discuss. Why is it tempting to make a story bigger? Why is it wrong?

**A second case** · a hard memory

> **[FIGURE: `u6-ethB`]** — *Some memories are painful — be gentle, and ask before you print.*

> **A case.** An old man tells Mira about the seven quiet years — how the road was empty, and how much he missed his family on the other side. He becomes sad, and his eyes fill with tears. Then he says, "Please, I do not want people to see me cry. Do not put that part in the story." It is a strong, human moment, and it would travel far on the wire. But the man asked Mira not to use it. The Code says: respect people, and be gentle with a hard memory. What does Mira do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**PRODUCE** — Discuss

## UNIT 7 · What Was Done: The Passive

**Beat · Report**  ·  CEFR A2 → lower B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. say what was done (past passive: was/were + done)
2. say what is done (present passive: is/are + done)
3. choose between active and passive
4. write a short report using the passive

**The story so far.** The families are back and the story of the seven years is told. Now Mira reports on the work itself: what was done to the bridge at Kalina, and who did it. In a report, the passive puts the result first — 'the bridge was rebuilt'.

### PART 2 · Grammar: the passive

*Was/were + done for the past, is/are + done for now.*

> **[FIGURE: `u7-gA`]** — *Active → passive: the result comes first.*

> **1 · Past passive — what was done**
>
> Form: {{was / were}} + past participle.
> The bridge {{was rebuilt}}.  The road {{was repaired}}.  New lamps {{were fitted}}.
> We use it to say what was done, when the result matters more than who did it.

> **2 · Active and passive**
>
> Active: Workers {{rebuilt}} the bridge.  (who + did + what)
> Passive: The bridge {{was rebuilt}} ({{by}} workers).  (what + was done)
> Add {{by}}… only if the doer matters. Often, we do not need it.

> **[FIGURE: `u7-gB`]** — *Present passive — for what is done again and again.*

> **3 · Present passive — what is done**
>
> Form: {{is / are}} + past participle.
> The wire {{is filed}} every hour.  The stalls {{are cleaned}} each morning.
> We use it for things that happen again and again.

**PRACTISE** — Structured practice

### PART 5 · Reading: the report

*Two readings. Read for what was done, and by whom.*

> **[FIGURE: `u7-read`]** — *The work on the bridge — and the people who did it.*

**Reading A** · a report on the rebuilding

> **A crossing rebuilt: the work at Kalina**
>
> A great deal of work was done at the Kalina crossing this year. According to the Crossing Office, the bridge was rebuilt and the road was repaired last April.
> The rail was painted, and the old gate was replaced. New lamps were fitted along the river, and the riverside path was cleared after seven years. Most of this work was done by local volunteers, with help from the councils on both sides.
> "Every week, something new is finished," said one volunteer, who worked on the bridge. "The gate was the hardest job. It was rusted shut for years, but now it opens every morning. Children walk through it on their way to school."
> Some work is still being done. This week, the school is being painted, and the riverside path is being cleaned. "The project is not complete," the office said, "but most of it is finished, and the crossing looks like a crossing again."
> The office asked to thank the volunteers by name. "The bridge was rebuilt by our neighbours — from both sides of the river," one worker said. "This was done by us, together. That is why it means so much."

> **[FIGURE: `g-model`]** — *A report reaches readers who want to know what was done — and by whom.*

**Reading B** · active or passive? — four tips

> **Four tips for the passive**
>
> **1. Use the passive for the result.** When the work matters more than the worker: 'The bridge was rebuilt.'
> **2. Use 'by…' when the doer matters.** 'The bridge was rebuilt by local volunteers.' Name people who should get credit.
> **3. Do not hide who did it.** 'Mistakes were made' hides the person. If readers should know who, say who.
> **4. Keep it clear.** The active voice is often shorter and clearer. Use the passive when it helps — not everywhere.

| use the past passive (was/were + done)? | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| ask who the work was done by? | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |

### PART 8 · Ethics: who did it?

*The passive can hide the doer. A fair report says who — when it matters.*

> **[FIGURE: `u7-ethA`]** — *'Mistakes were made' hides the person. If readers should know who, say who.*

**A first case** · hiding the doer

> **A case.** A part of the new river wall fell down a month after it was built. The building company sends Mira a line for the story: "A mistake was made, and the wall will be repaired." But the passive hides who made the mistake. Readers — and the families who live beside the wall — have a right to know which company built it. Mira can file the company's soft line, or she can find out who did the work and name them. The Code says: be accountable — do not use the passive to hide who is responsible. What does Mira do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8A**  Choose (a) or (b), and write one reason.

1. (a) file 'a mistake was made'  (b) find out who built the wall and name them.   Choice: ______  Because ________________________
2. 'A mistake was made' (no name) tells readers (a) who is responsible  (b) nothing about who.   Choice: ______

**8B**  Does it name who? Write Y (yes) or N (no).

1. "The wall was built by the Vara Company." ______
2. "A mistake was made." ______
3. "The office says the company will repair it." ______
4. "The wall fell down." ______

**PRACTISE** — Apply the Code

**8C**  Complete the rule. Use: hide · who · responsible · name.

> Do not use the passive to ______ the doer. When readers should know ______ is ______ , ______ them.

**PRODUCE** — Discuss

**8D**  Discuss. Why is 'mistakes were made' a problem in the news? Who does it protect?

**A second case** · who gets the credit

> **[FIGURE: `u7-ethB`]** — *Give credit fairly — to the people who did the work, not only the officials.*

> **A case.** The bridge was rebuilt mostly by local volunteers, who worked for four months. But an official asks Mira to write only that "the bridge was rebuilt by the councils." The councils helped and paid for materials, but the volunteers did most of the work. If Mira writes only 'by the councils', the volunteers get no credit — and the story goes out in six languages. The Code says: be fair and accurate — give credit to the people who really did the work. What does Mira do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

3. Do not forget the ___________ .
4. Write what is ___________ , not only what an official wants.

**PRODUCE** — Discuss

## UNIT 8 · What Has Happened: The Present Perfect

**Beat · Report & feature**  ·  CEFR A2 → lower B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. say what has happened (present perfect: has/have + done)
2. talk about a change with a result now
3. use for and since
4. use just, already, yet, ever and never

> **[FIGURE: `g-team`]** — *The Atlas Wire team — Mira reports on how the valley has changed.*

**The story so far.** The work is done and reported. Now Mira writes about the change itself: what has happened at Kalina, and how the valley has become a place where people live again. The present perfect links the past to the result we can see now.

### PART 1 · The words of change

*The words for talking about change. Learn these first.*

> **[FIGURE: `u8-words`]** — *Four key words — improve, recently, since, yet.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| change | to become different |
| improve | to get better |
| grow | to get bigger |
| become | to start to be |
| progress | moving forward; getting better |
| development | a new thing that happens |
| recently | a short time ago |
| since | from a time until now |
| for | for a length of time |
| already | before now |
| yet | until now (in questions and negatives) |
| just | a very short time ago |
| ever | at any time |
| never | at no time |

### PART 2 · Grammar: the present perfect

*Has/have + done for a past action with a result now.*

> **[FIGURE: `u8-gA`]** — *Present perfect — a past action with a result now.*

> **1 · Present perfect — what has happened**
>
> Form: {{has / have}} + past participle.
> The crossing {{has reopened}}.  Families {{have returned}}.  The valley {{has changed}}.
> We use it for a past action with a result now — the crossing is open now.

> **[FIGURE: `u8-gB`]** — *since + a point in time · for + a length of time.*

> **2 · for and since**
>
> {{since}} + a point in time: The valley has changed {{since}} the spring.
> {{for}} + a length of time: Families have been back {{for}} six months.
> Both go with the present perfect — from the past until now.

> **3 · just, already, yet, ever, never**
>
> {{just}}: The school has {{just}} reopened.   {{already}}: Families have {{already}} returned.
> {{yet}} (– / ?): The clinic has not reopened {{yet}}.
> {{ever}} / {{never}}: Have you {{ever}} visited?  I have {{never}} seen it so busy.

### PART 5 · Reading: a year of change

*Two readings. Read for what has changed, and what has not.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *A 'what has changed' feature — good news, and the work still to do.*

**Reading A** · how the valley has changed

> **How Kalina has changed**
>
> Kalina has changed a great deal since the spring. A year ago, the bridge was closed and the road was empty; today, people cross it from six in the morning. The market has reopened, and, according to the Crossing Office, a hundred families have returned to the valley.
> Life has improved in many small ways. The road has been repaired, the old gate has been replaced, and new lamps have been fitted along the river. The school itself has just reopened, and forty children have already gone back to class on the other side.
> "I have had my stall here since the spring," said Bekim, who sells fruit and vegetables on the bridge. "Every week is better than the last. The valley has become a home again. I have never been so busy."
> But not everything has changed yet. The clinic is still closed, and the bus does not cross the bridge yet. "We have done a lot," the Crossing Office said, "but we have not finished. There is still work to do."
> For the people of Kalina, the change is easy to see. In one year, a quiet, empty crossing has become a busy road again — and, they say, the best is still to come.

> **[FIGURE: `u8-read`]** — *Five dates that have changed how the world talks about press freedom. Sources: UNESCO; Reporters Without Borders.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-model`]** — *A change story feels close to readers, because the result is now.*

**Reading B** · present perfect or past simple? — four tips

> **Four tips for the present perfect**
>
> **1. Use the present perfect for a result now.** 'The crossing has reopened.' (and it is open now).
> **2. Use the past simple for a finished time.** 'The crossing reopened last April.' (a finished time — last April).
> **3. Use since and for.** 'since the spring' (a point) / 'for six months' (a length). Both link to now.
> **4. Report both sides.** Say what has improved — and what has not changed yet. That is fair and accurate.

### PART 8 · Ethics: the whole picture

*Good news is real — but so are the problems. Report both.*

> **[FIGURE: `u8-ethA`]** — *'It has fully recovered' is a claim — not a fact until it is true.*

**A first case** · 'fully recovered'

> **A case.** An official gives Mira a happy line: "Write that Kalina has fully recovered, and everything is finished." It would be a bright, positive headline on an international wire. But it is not accurate. The clinic has not reopened yet, there is no bus, and some families have not returned. A lot has improved — but the valley has not 'fully recovered'. Mira knows the Code: be accurate. Progress is not the same as 'finished'. What does Mira write?

### PART 2 · Grammar: advice and rules

*Should for advice, must and have to for rules.*

> **[FIGURE: `u9-gA`]** — *should / shouldn't — for advice.*

> **1 · should — advice**
>
> {{You should}} + verb: {{You should}} check every fact.
> {{You shouldn't}} + verb: {{You shouldn't}} guess.
> We use *should* to give advice — a good idea, not a strong rule.

> **2 · must / have to — rules**
>
> {{must}} = a strong rule: You {{must}} protect your source.
> {{have to}} = it is necessary: You {{have to}} meet the deadline.
> [[must not]] = it is forbidden: You {{must not}} file a rumour.

> **[FIGURE: `u9-gB`]** — *must = a strong rule · have to = it is necessary.*

> **3 · Which one?**
>
> Advice (a good idea): You {{should}} ask a follow-up question.
> A rule (you have no choice): You {{must}} name your source.
> Not necessary: You {{don't have to}} file it today, but you can.

**PRACTISE** — Structured practice

**2A**  Give advice. Complete with should or shouldn't.

1. You ___________ check the facts.

### PART 5 · Reading: the rules

*Two readings. Read for the advice and the rules.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *Advice for a new correspondent — what to do, and what will follow.*

**Reading A** · advice for a new correspondent

> **Ten minutes of advice: a note for a new correspondent**
>
> On Sofia's first day at Atlas Wire, Mira gave her a short note of advice. "I have been a correspondent for many years," she wrote, "and this is what I have learned."
> "First, you should check every fact. If you check, your story will be strong. If you rush and guess, you will make mistakes, and readers will not trust you. So take your time — it is better to be right than to be first."
> "Second, there are rules you must follow. You must protect your source. You have to be honest, and you must not file a rumour as a fact. If you break these rules, you will lose the one thing a journalist really has: trust."
> "Third, when you work in a country that is not your own, you should listen before you write. Learn how the place works. Get your accreditation early. And remember that the local journalist beside you knows more than you do — you should ask them, and you must credit them."
> "And last: if you make a mistake, you must say sorry and correct it. Everyone makes mistakes. A good reporter is not the one who never fails, but the one who always tells the truth about it."

**PRACTISE** — Comprehension

> **[FIGURE: `u9-read`]** — *Four rules that hold in every newsroom, in every country.*

**Reading B** · four things you must do

> **The rules of the newsroom**
>
> **1. You must check every fact.** If you are not sure, ask, or leave it out. Do not guess.
> **2. You must protect your source.** If a source is not safe, you must keep their name out of the story.
> **3. You have to be fair.** Give both sides. If you only give one side, the story is not fair.
> **4. You should fix your mistakes.** If you make a mistake, say sorry and correct it. Readers will trust you more, not less.

### PART 8 · Ethics: the rules that matter

*Some rules are not just advice — they protect people. You must follow them.*

> **[FIGURE: `u9-ethA`]** — *A deadline is not a reason to break a rule.*

**A first case** · the deadline and the fact

> **A case.** It is Sofia's first big story, and the wire goes in ten minutes. She has a strong line, but she has not checked one number. Her editor is waiting. She thinks: "If I check, I will miss the deadline. If I don't check, maybe it is fine." But the rule is clear: you must check every fact. If she files a wrong number, it will go out to outlets in many countries, readers will be misled, and the agency will lose trust. Sofia knows the Code: you should never break a rule to be fast. What should Sofia do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8A**  Choose (a) or (b), and write one reason.

1. (a) file it now, unchecked  (b) check first, even if the story is a little late.   Choice: ______  Because ________________________
2. If she files a wrong number, readers will be (a) helped  (b) misled.   Choice: ______

**8B**  Should or must? Write S or M.

2. Ask a follow-up question. ______
3. Protect your source. ______
4. Read the wire every morning. ______

**PRACTISE** — Apply the Code

**A second case** · your local colleague

> **[FIGURE: `u9-ethB`]** — *A colleague's safety comes before a stronger byline.*

> **A case.** Dren, a journalist who lives at Kalina, has found most of Sofia's story. He knows everyone, he arranged the interviews, and he translated them. Now the desk wants a byline. Dren says, "Please do not put my name on it. I live here, and I will still be here when you go home." Another reporter says, "Use his name — it makes the story stronger, and it is his work." Sofia knows the Code: credit the people who did the work, but a colleague's safety comes first, and it is their decision, not yours. What should Sofia do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**Beat · Capstone**  ·  CEFR A2 → lower B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| front page | the first page of a newspaper |
| masthead | the newspaper's name at the top |
| headline | the big title |
| byline | the line with the writer's name |
| dateline | the place and date at the start of a report |
| lead | the first sentence of a story |
| caption | the words under a photo |
| layout | how a page is arranged |
| edit | to check and improve a story |
| publish | to make public; to print |
| column | a tall block of text |
| describe | to say what someone or something is like |
| connect | to join two ideas |
| final | the last |

### PART 2 · Grammar: relative clauses

*who for people, which/that for things, where for places.*

> **[FIGURE: `u10-gA`]** — *who = people · which / that = things.*

> **1 · who / which / that**
>
> {{who}} for people: The correspondent {{who}} wrote the story is Mira.
> {{which}} / {{that}} for things: The story {{that}} everyone read.  The photograph {{which}} we chose.
> We use them to say which person or thing we mean.

> **[FIGURE: `u10-gB`]** — *where — for places.*

> **2 · where**
>
> {{where}} for places: Kalina is the town {{where}} the families came back.
> This is the desk {{where}} the team works.
> Use *where* to join a place to what happened there.

> **3 · Joining two ideas**
>
> Two sentences: Mira is a correspondent. She wrote the story.
> One sentence: Mira is a correspondent {{who}} wrote the story.
> Joining ideas makes your writing flow, and is better to read.

### PART 5 · Reading: the front page

*Two readings. Read for the story, and for the parts of the page.*

> **[FIGURE: `u10-read`]** — *The front page that told the whole story.*

**Reading A** · the story that brought a town home

> **A crossing comes home**
>
> **By Mira Sandoval, Atlas Wire · KALINA**
> Kalina, the town that was quiet for seven years, is a home again. The bridge, which reopened last April, is busy every morning, and the families who left have come back.
> The correspondent who followed the story all year is Mira Sandoval. "I have watched this valley change," she said. "The road that was empty is full of children, and the stalls that disappeared have come back."
> Much of the work was done by the volunteers who live here, on both sides of the river. Elena Marku, who owns the café at the end of the bridge, is one of them. "It is our home," she said — words that many people in the valley now repeat.
> According to the Crossing Office, a hundred families have returned. There is still work to do: the clinic, which is closed, has not reopened yet. But the change is easy to see.
> This is the front page that tells the story — a story about a place where, after seven quiet years, the people came home. As Elena said, and as the headline now reads: the crossing has come home.

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *One front page can tell a whole year's story, in many countries at once.*

**Reading B** · making a front page — the parts

> **The parts of a front page**
>
> **1. Masthead and headline.** The masthead is the paper's name at the top. The headline is the big title that people read first.
> **2. Byline and dateline.** The byline names the writer. The dateline says where the report comes from — on an international page, it is the first thing a reader looks for.
> **3. Lead, photograph and caption.** The lead is the first sentence, which gives the five Ws. A strong photograph, and a caption which says what the photograph shows.
> **4. Edit and check.** Before you publish, edit the page: check every fact, every name, and every quote. A front page that has a mistake loses trust.

### PART 8 · Ethics: the whole Code

*The front page brings the whole Code together: accurate, fair, and kind.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-code`]** — *Five words that have held this course together, and now hold one page together.*

> **[FIGURE: `u10-ethA`]** — *The lead story is the important one — not the loudest one.*

**A first case** · which story leads?

> **A case.** The team has two stories. One is the town that has come home — an important, true story that helps readers in many countries understand the year. The other is a small, shocking claim that would be shared more widely, but that nobody has checked. An editor says, "Put the shocking one on the front — it will travel further." But it is a rumour, and it is not the story that matters most. The Code says: choose the story that is important and true, not the one that is loud. Which story does the team put on the front page?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8A**  Choose (a) or (b), and write one reason.

1. (a) the shocking, unchecked claim  (b) the important, true story.   Choice: ______  Because ________________________
2. A front page should carry the story that is (a) loudest  (b) most important and true.   Choice: ______

**8B**  Front page or not? Write Y (yes) or N (no).

1. An important, checked, true story. ______
2. A shocking claim nobody has checked. ______
3. A story that helps readers understand. ______
4. A story chosen only because it will be shared. ______

**PRACTISE** — Apply the Code

**PRODUCE** — Discuss

**8D**  Discuss. Why should a newspaper not choose its front page only to be shared more widely?

**A second case** · a correction on the front

> **[FIGURE: `u10-ethB`]** — *If the front page had a mistake, correct it — in public.*

> **A case.** Yesterday's front page had a small mistake: it gave the wrong number of families. A reader found it, and the reader is right. The story went out on the wire, so outlets in six countries printed the wrong number too. Someone says, "It was small. Just fix it quietly online, and say nothing." But the mistake was on the front page, where everyone saw it. The Code says: be honest — if you make a public mistake, you correct it in public, and you tell everyone who used it. What does the team do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

### PART 11 · Final project: your front page

*Bring the whole course together. Make a complete front page.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-template`]** — *The template — build your front page part by part.*

**Your task. **Make a full front page for a story of your choice (real or invented). Use everything you have learned this course. Work alone or in a small team — a correspondent, a photographer, and an editor.

> **[FIGURE: `g-frontpage-parts`]** — *Every part of the page, and what it is for.*

**Your front page must have:**

1. a **masthead** (your outlet's name) and a strong **headline** (5–7 words) — Units 1 & 10;
2. a **byline** (By…) and a **dateline** (the place you are reporting from) — Units 1 & 10;
3. a **lead** sentence that gives the five Ws — Units 2 & 6;
4. a short **story** that reports what happened and what has changed — Units 6, 7 & 8;
5. at least one **exact quote**, with attribution ('… said' / 'according to…') — Units 4 & 5;
6. a **photo box** and a **caption** — Unit 10;
7. at least two **relative clauses** (who / which / that / where) — Unit 10.

> **[FIGURE: `g-model`]** — *A model — use it, and Reading A, to check the shape of your page.*

> Before you publish, edit it. Check every fact, every name, and every quote. Be accurate, fair, and kind. Lead with the story that is important and true — not the one that is loud. That is the whole Code, on one page.

| Success criteria — the whole course | Yes | Almost | Not yet |
|---|---|---|---|
| It has a masthead, a headline, a byline and a dateline. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| The lead gives the five Ws. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| It has one exact quote, with a named source. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| It uses the past, the passive, or the present perfect correctly. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| It uses at least two relative clauses. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| It is edited: every fact, name, and quote is checked. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| It is accurate, fair, and kind. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |

**Congratulations. **You have finished English for Journalists. You started by learning the words of the newsroom; now you can plan, write, edit, and publish a front page — in English, in any country, and with a journalist's care for the truth. A free press, in plain English.
